query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high‐entropy alloy (HEA) system—in which the large configurational entropy and associated atomic size mismatches suppress nucleation of crystals—can be used to enhance glass‐forming ability. In other words, a melt of a single‐phase HEA (for example, a low–Al content CoCrFeNi alloy) can be more readily quenched into a glassy (amorphous) state than a conventional alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase molten high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic or near‐equiatomic CoCrFeNi-based system) with high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Rapid quenching of the melt under inert conditions to bypass crystallization.
generation.conditions: A sufficiently high cooling rate in an inert atmosphere (to avoid oxidation) with melt homogenization achieved at temperatures above the liquidus.
generation.structural_mediator: High configurational entropy that both favors a single‐phase liquid state and, together with significant atomic size differences and low diffusion rates (sluggish diffusion), kinetically suppresses crystallization during cooling.
generation.mechanism: The presence of multiple principal elements creates a thermodynamic landscape where the driving force for nucleation is reduced. Combined with sluggish atomic mobility, this delays or prevents crystallization during rapid cooling, thereby promoting glass formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical quenching conditions, the high‐entropy alloy will exhibit an enhanced glass‐forming ability (i.e. lower critical cooling rate and absence of long-range crystalline order) compared to a conventional melt with lower configurational entropy.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloy melts with one or two principal elements that have lower configurational entropy and faster diffusion, which crystallize more readily upon cooling.
generation.boundary: The effect depends on achieving a sufficiently uniform melt and requires that the chosen HEA composition combines proper atomic size mismatches and moderate mixing enthalpies; overly strong intermetallic tendencies or insufficient atomic size differ­ences may negate the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: While the high-entropy effect suggests enhanced glass-forming ability, direct quantitative evidence (e.g., measured critical cooling rates or glass transition behaviors) for such HEAs remains to be established, making the precise magnitude of the effect uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy systems: one a high-entropy alloy (for example, a well-homogenized low-Al content CoCrFeNi alloy) and the other a conventional alloy with similar melting temperature but lower configurational entropy. Melt both alloys under identical conditions and quench them using a controlled, high cooling rate process in an inert atmosphere. Characterize the resulting solidified structures using X-ray diffraction (XRD), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to detect the presence or absence of crystallinity.
measurements: XRD to assess if an amorphous hump (indicative of glass formation) is present or if crystalline peaks are observed
DSC to determine the presence of a glass transition temperature (Tg) and crystallization exotherms
TEM to examine the microstructure for nanoscale crystalline regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a lower critical cooling rate (i.e., if it crystallizes under the same quenching conditions as the conventional alloy) or fails to form an amorphous structure as evidenced by XRD, DSC, and TEM, then the hypothesis that the HEA enhances glass-forming ability is falsified.
